tldr: We propose Fiber, a framework that projects heterogeneous expert policies into the latent space of a Behavioral Foundation Model (BFM) by aligning their output actions. This bridges low-frequency perceptive flow planning with high-frequency whole-body control. Fiber dramatically outperforms existing baselines in simulation and successfully demonstrates seamless chaining across diverse tasks—from opening heavy doors to picking and carrying boxes—on a real Unitree G1 humanoid.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of Fiber. It consists of three stages: (a) heterogeneously acquired task experts, (b) Latent Policy Projection (LPP) that maps expert control responses into the latent space of a frozen AH-BFM, and (c) a single perceptive flow planner trained offline on aggregated rollouts.
overview:
When teaching humanoid robots diverse whole-body loco-manipulation tasks, a major bottleneck is designing the representation connecting high-level task planning and low-level contact feedback control. If geometric targets like end-effector trajectories are used, state-dependent physical compliance against contacts and disturbances is often lost. On the other hand, if a high-level planner directly predicts low-level actions, it must shoulder the burden of modeling high-frequency feedback control, which quickly breaks down in contact-rich tasks.

To solve this, the authors introduce Fiber, a framework that uses the executable latent space of a pretrained Behavioral Foundation Model (BFM) as a shared action interface. The core idea is Latent Policy Projection (LPP), which directly aligns the outputs of independently trained task experts with the physical joint targets (actions) generated by the BFM. This enables heterogeneous skills with vastly different observation spaces and reward designs to be unified into a single latent space while preserving their physical responses. Furthermore, the authors propose an Adaptive-Horizon BFM (AH-BFM) that reconciles short-term precision with long-term behavioral consistency, and train an offline flow matching planner on aggregated latent rollouts.

Evaluated across 128 diverse environment variations per task in simulation, Fiber achieved an average success rate of 42.0%, substantially outperforming kinematic planning (3.5%) and projected latent replay (11.6%). On a physical Unitree G1 humanoid, Fiber demonstrated zero-shot sim-to-real transfer, dynamic skill chaining (e.g., opening a heavy door, picking up a box, and carrying it), and robust self-recovery from stumbling while carrying a load.
contributions: A unified planning framework using the executable latent space of a frozen BFM as a shared representation, enabling low-frequency high-level planning while retaining high-frequency whole-body state feedback.
Latent Policy Projection (LPP), which projects local control responses of independently trained heterogeneous experts into the BFM latent space by matching their induced physical actions.
An Adaptive-Horizon BFM (AH-BFM) trained with multi-$\gamma$ FB learning to resolve the trade-off between short-term precise tracking and long-term behavioral consistency.
Demonstrations on a real humanoid robot (Unitree G1) showing perceptive sim-to-real transfer, dynamic multi-skill chaining, and active disturbance recovery.

sections.heading: What is the right representation connecting humanoid planning and control?
sections.summary: Building generalist humanoids that handle diverse whole-body tasks requires a representation reconciling high-level decision-making with high-frequency physical feedback control. This section discusses the limitations of both geometric targets and direct action prediction, introducing Fiber and its use of a pretrained BFM latent space.
sections.details:
Humanoid loco-manipulation is both a cognitive task that decides what to do based on visual scenes and a demanding physical control task that coordinates the entire body while balancing and handling contacts.

Traditional hierarchical approaches typically have a high-level planner predict end-effector positions or contact targets while a low-level controller tracks them. However, even when reaching for the same hand position, the required joint torques and commands vary drastically depending on contact states, object weights, or external disturbances. In short, purely kinematic targets cannot fully encode the state-dependent control responses needed for physical interaction. Conversely, requiring the planner to directly predict high-frequency low-level actions forces it to model massive closed-loop contact corrections, making offline learning exceptionally difficult.

Here is the key insight. The authors turn to Behavioral Foundation Models (BFMs), which take the robot's state and a latent command to generate high-frequency joint actions. The latent representation of a BFM is not merely a target trajectory; it serves as an index that specifies an entire state-dependent control policy. Thus, the planner only needs to generate compact latent commands at a low frequency, leaving high-frequency physical feedback to the BFM.

To integrate diverse skills into this shared space, the paper introduces Latent Policy Projection (LPP). After acquiring individual skills via reinforcement learning or other methods, LPP aligns their output actions to map disparate experts into a unified latent space. This paves the way toward safely and scalably training a single perceptive planner across all skills.

sections.heading: Lineage of whole-body foundation controllers and loco-manipulation
sections.summary: This section reviews recent progress in whole-body foundation controllers, Behavioral Foundation Models (BFMs), and task representations for loco-manipulation. It highlights the limits of existing distillation and structured target methods, contextualizing how Fiber unifies standalone skills post-hoc via a frozen BFM.
sections.details:
### II-A Humanoid Controllers and Behavioral Foundation Models
Recent research has shifted from designing separate controllers per motor skill toward unified controllers that cover walking and broad whole-body movements in a single model. In particular, works such as BFM-Zero demonstrated that Forward-Backward (FB) representation learning can build promptable behavioral latent spaces. However, existing latent exploration techniques primarily target steady-state motions or desired kinematic trajectory tracking. They are insufficient for capturing dynamic feedback in manipulation, where contacts and forces change rapidly. Moreover, standard FB learning suffers from a trade-off between local precise tracking and long-term behavioral maintenance, which this paper's Adaptive-Horizon BFM (AH-BFM) directly addresses.

### II-B Loco-Manipulation and Task Representations
Structured representations—such as contact sequences, end-effector constraints, and distance fields—have been widely explored to describe contact-rich tasks. While interpretable, they rely on hand-engineered variables and cannot directly express subtle, state-dependent control responses arising from contact dynamics. On the other hand, end-to-end reinforcement learning or imitation learning can acquire these responses, but the resulting policies remain tied to specific task setups. Online multi-task distillation across experts is promising, yet keeping all simulation environments active simultaneously is prohibitively heavy and hard to scale. This work sets itself apart by decoupling skill acquisition from skill integration, bridging them through the native action space of a frozen BFM.

sections.heading: How Fiber works: latent projection, adaptive BFM, and unified flow planning
sections.summary: Fiber consists of three stages: (1) heterogeneous skill acquisition, (2) Latent Policy Projection (LPP) via action alignment, and (3) offline training of a perceptive flow planner. This section details how AH-BFM dynamically blends short and long horizons, as well as how motion reuse via Successor Features works.
sections.details:
### III-A Overall Pipeline
Fiber's workflow is straightforward. First, task-specific expert policies are trained independently using the most suitable method for each task. Next, LPP projects each expert's local control responses into the latent space of a frozen BFM. Once projected, the original expert environments can be discarded. Finally, a single offline perceptive flow planner is trained on the aggregated latent rollouts produced by the projected policies.

### III-B Heterogeneous Skill Acquisition Routes
Experts can be obtained through the most effective route per task:
- **Motion Imitation-Based:** When human or object reference trajectories exist (such as object grasping and lifting), RL is trained with tracking and contact rewards.
- **Reward-Engineered:** When clear reference motions are unavailable (such as opening a door), RL is trained from scratch using staged rewards for approaching, contacting, turning the handle, and opening.
- **Successor Feature (SF) Motion Reuse:** Combines pre-existing BFM whole-body behaviors (e.g., crouching or running) with manipulation. By adding a lightweight latent adapter on top of the frozen BFM, this method simultaneously maximizes the task reward $r_t^I$ and alignment with a native latent vector $z^N$ (the SF term), efficiently discovering composite behaviors like crouching while carrying a box.

### III-C Action-Aligned Latent Policy Projection (LPP)
How do we map independently trained experts into a single latent space? This is the core mechanism. At each update interval, a projector $P_{\psi_i}$ outputs a latent vector $z_k$, which is spherically interpolated (SLERP) between steps and fed into the BFM. An action alignment loss is introduced to minimize the error between the joint targets generated by the BFM and the physical joint targets output by the expert. To resolve ambiguities where multiple latent vectors yield similar actions, a semantic regularization term pulls the latent vector toward the BFM's backward representation $B(s)$ via cosine similarity. Training follows a DAgger-style on-policy data aggregation, ensuring robust recovery even when states deviate from expert trajectories.

### III-D Adaptive-Horizon BFM (AH-BFM) and Flow Planner
A planning latent space requires both short horizons ($\gamma_s$) for precise local tracking and long horizons ($\gamma_l$) for whole-body stability and behavioral consistency. AH-BFM elegantly satisfies both by performing normalized FB learning per discount factor $\gamma$ and adaptively blending actor gradient weights based on state and latent inputs. Using latent rollouts aggregated from all skills, a Diffusion Transformer (DiT) flow matching planner is trained entirely offline, conditioned on depth images, proprioception, and language or waypoint steering tokens.

sections.heading: Validation in sim and on the real G1: generalization and real-world adaptation
sections.summary: Fiber was evaluated on box pickup, door opening, and object grasping. It achieved a 42.0% mean success rate across 128 simulation variations per task, and demonstrated dynamic whole-body coordination, continuous skill chaining, and active disturbance recovery on a real Unitree G1 humanoid.
sections.details:
### IV-A Simulation Evaluation
Rigorous evaluations were conducted in IsaacSim across 128 diverse variations per task, including box sizes and positions, door handle geometries, and graspable object shapes.

- **Expert Projection Fidelity (Q1):** Projected policies via LPP matched the original experts' performance on box pickup and door opening. However, on object grasping requiring fine fingertip precision, success dropped from 97.0% (expert) to 52.9%, highlighting the challenge of latent projection for delicate contacts.
- **Unified Planner Comparison (Q2):** The unified perceptive planner, Fiber, achieved a 42.0% average success rate. In contrast, open-loop replay of projected latents managed only 11.6%, proving that low-frequency perceptive feedback (replanning) is essential. Directly predicting joint actions from the planner (Action Planner) failed completely at 0%, and Kinematic Planner tracking end-effector goals yielded only 3.5%. The force-adaptive tracking baseline, FALCON, managed just 0.4%–2.7% on door opening.
- **Skill Chaining (Q3):** As shown in Figure F2, a single unified policy seamlessly executed the sequence of opening a door, entering the room, picking up a box, and carrying it back out, guided solely by switching high-level conditioning commands.

### IV-B Real Humanoid Deployment (Unitree G1)
The model was transferred zero-shot from simulation to a physical Unitree G1 equipped with an onboard RealSense depth camera. The entire pipeline ran real-time on a single laptop (NVIDIA RTX PRO 5000 Blackwell), running the flow planner at 5 Hz (~20 ms inference) and the BFM at 50 Hz (~1 ms inference).

Real-world trials achieved 6/10 successes for box pickup and 4/10 for door opening (2/10 for small object grasping due to depth noise). Crucially, because planned latent commands interact directly with the BFM's high-frequency feedback loop, natural adaptive behaviors emerged (Figure F3): the robot repositioned its hands underneath when a box began to slip, and leaned its entire body weight forward when pushing open a heavy door. When the robot stumbled heavily and dropped to one knee while carrying a box, it recovered its balance without dropping the load and resumed walking.

### IV-C Ablation Studies (Q4)
Evaluating AH-BFM revealed that replacing a fixed-horizon BFM ($\gamma=0.98$) with AH-BFM boosted LPP average success from 68.8% to 72.8%. Furthermore, action-aligned LPP significantly outperformed state-only $B(s)$ tracking, confirming that matching control responses in physical action space is vital for unifying interaction skills.

sections.heading: Conclusions and what comes next: expanding to more dynamic whole-body behaviors
sections.summary: Fiber establishes a novel paradigm to unify heterogeneous skills without sacrificing high-frequency physical feedback through action alignment and adaptive-horizon BFMs. Future work includes expanding to dynamic locomotion on stairs, integrating tactile feedback, and incorporating online latent adaptation.
sections.details:
This paper presented Fiber, a unified framework for versatile humanoid loco-manipulation. Projecting independently acquired heterogeneous experts into the latent space of a frozen BFM via action-space response matching, followed by offline perceptive planner training, provides a scalable and physically compliant solution.

The authors also candidly highlight limitations and future directions. First, the current BFM assumes flat-ground locomotion; extending it to highly dynamic behaviors like stair climbing or jumping on uneven terrain is necessary. Second, as seen in fine-grained object grasping, noisy onboard depth data and contact uncertainty call for integrating tactile and force-torque sensors alongside vision. Third, because the framework currently does not optimize latent commands online during deployment, adding test-time latent adaptation could further improve responsiveness to unexpected contact dynamics in the real world.

sections.heading: Appendix: AH-BFM formulation and tricks for real-time robot execution
sections.summary: The appendix provides mathematical stability proofs for multi-horizon FB learning, expert projection architectures, the planner's DiT setup, and Real-Time Chunking (RTC) which prevents discontinuities during physical deployment.
sections.details:
### Appendix A: AH-BFM Stability and Architecture
AH-BFM uses a latent dimension of $d_z=256$, normalized on a hypersphere of radius $\sqrt{d_z}$. Actor inputs total 930 dimensions, combining current proprioception with a 9-frame history. In multi-horizon FB learning, normalized objectives $(1-\gamma) Q_\gamma^{\mathrm{FB}}$ per discount factor $\gamma$ are aggregated via softmax-based adaptive weighting. Theoretical analysis in the appendix proves that this normalized FB Bellman operator is non-expansive, guaranteeing stable updates where perturbations do not amplify across horizons.

### Appendices B & C: Expert Projection and Common Action Spaces
While experts differ in observation spaces and action scaling, actions are converted to a unified physical space of 29-DoF target joint positions (radians) for the robot's PD controllers before computing the action alignment loss. The projector consists of a residual MLP that updates latent vectors at 10 Hz (every 0.1 s) with SLERP interpolation between steps. For hand manipulation (14-DoF Dex3 hands), an isolated head directly predicts joint targets independently of the BFM's whole-body latent space.

### Appendices D & E: Planner Architecture and Real-Time Chunking (RTC)
The offline planner is a Diffusion Transformer (DiT) conditioned on 192 spatial patch tokens extracted from a 144×256 depth image, proprioceptive tokens, and language/waypoint steering tokens, predicting a 1-second (10-step) latent chunk.

A vital mechanism for physical deployment is Real-Time Chunking (RTC). When regenerating trajectories at 5 Hz with flow matching, new predictions temporally overlap with the previous chunk. RTC smoothly guides the overlapping section toward the earlier trajectory during numerical flow integration. As a result, command trajectories remain continuous across replanning intervals (handling ~20 ms inference latency), delivering smooth and uninterrupted physical execution.

takeaways: Instead of geometric goals or direct actions, the executable latent space of a pretrained foundation model (BFM) serves as an ideal interface between high-level planning and low-level control.
Even when expert policies are trained across completely different setups and rewards, aligning their physical joint commands enables consistent projection into a single latent space.
Adaptive-Horizon learning (AH-BFM) with multiple discount factors is key to reconciling local high-precision tracking with long-term whole-body stability.

Decoupling a low-frequency perceptive flow planner (5 Hz) from a high-frequency foundation controller (50 Hz) significantly reduces computational burden while sustaining contact-rich adaptive behaviors on real hardware.
limitations: In tasks requiring millimeter-level precision, such as fine object grasping, success rates drop noticeably due to latent projection loss and onboard depth sensor noise.
The current BFM is restricted to flat-ground locomotion; expanding to dynamic, acrobatic motions like rough terrain navigation or stair climbing remains future work.
There is currently no test-time online latent adaptation mechanism to adjust to unmodeled contact dynamics on the fly.
